nameStory: Estuary Beggarticks gets its name from two key features: it thrives in estuaries where fresh and salt water mix, and its seeds are notorious "beggars" that grab onto clothing and fur with tiny barbed hooks. The "ticks" part refers to how tenaciously these seeds stick to anything that brushes against them, much like the blood-sucking parasites they're named after.
description: Estuary Beggarticks is a variable annual herb that grows in the salty margins where rivers meet the sea. This member of the sunflower family produces cheerful yellow daisy-like flowers that brighten up coastal marshes in late summer. The plant has a somewhat scraggly appearance with branching stems and can vary considerably in size depending on growing conditions. It's one of the rarer beggarticks in New England, specially adapted to handle the challenging conditions of estuarine environments.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright yellow daisy-like flowers with both ray petals (the outer "petals") and central disk flowers, blooming from late summer into fall. Flowers feel papery when touched and have a faint honey-like scent.

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Found exclusively in salt marshes and estuarine areas where most other plants can't survive. The salty, muddy soil and tidal influence are key identifying clues that you've found this rare species.

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Flat, dark brown seeds topped with 2-4 barbed bristles that feel sharp and grabby when touched. These "beggartick" seeds cling tenaciously to clothing, fur, and skin with their backward-pointing hooks.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Variable annual herb that can be quite small and compact in harsh conditions or more robust and branching in favorable spots. Stems often have a reddish tinge and feel somewhat succulent due to salt adaptation.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Leaves are typically narrow and may be toothed or divided, with a slightly thick, fleshy texture that helps the plant cope with salt stress. They feel smooth but substantial between your fingers.

habitat: Estuary Beggarticks is found exclusively in salt marshes, estuarine mudflats, and tidal shores where fresh and salt water mix. Look for it in the challenging environment of coastal wetlands where few other flowering plants can tolerate the salty conditions and tidal fluctuations. In New England, it's most likely to be found along protected coastlines and river mouths.

seasonality.spring: Seeds germinate in the muddy marsh substrate as temperatures warm. Young plants are small and inconspicuous, focusing energy on establishing roots in the challenging saline environment.
seasonality.summer: Plants grow vegetatively, developing their characteristic branching habit and thick, salt-adapted leaves. Flower buds begin forming in mid to late summer.
seasonality.fall: Peak blooming time when the bright yellow flowers are most visible and diagnostic. Seeds mature and develop their characteristic barbed bristles, becoming sticky hitchhikers ready to disperse.
seasonality.winter: Annual plants die back completely, leaving only seeds to overwinter in the marsh mud. The habitat remains identifiable by its characteristic estuarine features.

funFact: This plant is like the maritime survivalist of the beggarticks family - it's one of the few members that has evolved special adaptations to handle salt water, making it tough enough to thrive where most land plants would quickly die from salt poisoning.
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with Nodding Beggarticks or Smooth Beggarticks, but the habitat is the key difference - if you're not standing in a salt marsh or estuary, you're probably looking at a different species. The salty, tidal environment is this plant's signature calling card.
contextualKnowledge: This is one of New England's rarest wildflowers, listed as endangered in Massachusetts and possibly gone from New Hampshire entirely. Finding one is a special botanical discovery that should be reported to local naturalist groups, as every population is important for the species' survival.
compareHints: Unlike its freshwater cousins like Devil's Beggarticks or Nodding Beggarticks, Estuary Beggarticks has evolved to handle salt stress, giving it thicker, more succulent leaves and limiting it to coastal habitats. While the yellow flowers look similar to Smooth Beggarticks and Nodding Beggarticks, the estuarine habitat immediately sets it apart from all other beggarticks species in New England.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's many beggarticks species, Devil's Beggarticks is distinguished by its three-part leaves (versus simple leaves in Nodding Beggarticks) and its lack of showy petals (unlike the bright yellow rays of Tickseed Sunflower).

Among New England's many beggarticks species, Nodding Beggarticks is the easiest to identify because of its drooping flowers - Devil's Beggarticks has upward-facing flowers and deeply divided leaves, while Smooth Beggarticks has much larger, showier flowers that face outward.
Among New England's many beggarticks species, Purplestem stands out for its smooth stems with purple coloring and relatively few flower heads per plant.
Unlike its weedy beggarticks relatives that grow in damp soil and are known for their sticky seeds, Water Marigold is the aquatic specialist of the family.
Among New England's beggarticks, Tall Beggarticks stands out for its height and hairy stems.

Among its many Bidens relatives in New England, Smooth Beggarticks stands out for its simple, undivided leaves (unlike Three-parted Beggarticks) and its prominent yellow ray petals (unlike Devil's Beggarticks which often lacks showy petals entirely).

Among its many beggarticks relatives, swamp beggarticks stands out for its complete lack of ray petals (the showy outer petals), unlike nodding beggarticks or smooth beggarticks which have yellow rays.

Among New England beggarticks, Three-parted is unique for its deeply three-divided leaves - Devil's Beggarticks has simple oval leaves, while Spanish Needles has finely divided, almost fern-like foliage.
Among New England's many beggarticks species, Tickseed Sunflower stands out for having showy yellow petals - many of its relatives like Devil's Beggarticks have tiny or no petals at all.

Among its beggarticks relatives, Spanish needles stands out with its finely divided, feathery leaves - most other Bidens species have simple oval leaves or leaves divided into just 3-5 broad segments.
Among New England's beggarticks, Bearded Beggarticks stands out for its large, showy yellow petals - most other species like Devil's Beggarticks have tiny or no petals at all.

Marsh Tickseed stands out from its beggarticks relatives by being strictly a wetland specialist - while cousins like Devil's Beggarticks grow in disturbed soils and gardens, Marsh Tickseed demands consistently soggy conditions.
Among its many beggarticks relatives, Eaton's is unique for its salt marsh habitat - most others prefer freshwater wetlands or disturbed soils.
White beggarticks stands out from its many beggarticks relatives because of its prominent white petals - most other species in the genus have small, inconspicuous flowers or yellow petals.
